goals:
My goals in developing this guide have been to:
  • To provide easy & immediate access to literary, cultural & historical information that helps a modern reader to understand (as much as possible) what each significant word, phrase, sentence &/or passage would have communicated to an original reader in their context:
    • the general background information is provided in the 'introduction' pages, particularly those on the Jewish, Roman & Christian contexts of the Apocalypse
    • information relevant to each specific passage in Revelation is available through links on the relevant page within the guide.
  • To prompt & guide readers through a process of contemplative reading, understanding & digesting what each passage reveals:
    • the text is broken out of the usual 'verse & passage' formats in modern translations;
    • visual mapping is used to lay out key ideas & connections so that repeated &/or related concepts/assertions are aligned &/or grouped;
    • room is provided to allow notes (from the comments &/or our own thoughts & insights) to be easily added.
assumptions:
Western Christians often bring modern American, Eurocentric &/or post-Enlightenment assumptions to the text that ignore or distort the original message given in the first-century Mediterranean context.

Common assumptions include:
  • Chronological linearism
    (the 'Timeline' assumption)
  • Radical individualism
  • Strict literalism
  • Modernist political/geopolitical framing
  • Escapism
    (the 'Rapture' lens)
linearism:
[Back]

Many Western readers assume the book is a linear, chronological roadmap of future world history. Because Western culture views time as a straight line moving from point A to point B, readers expect Revelation to unfold sequentially. In contrast, ancient Near Eastern & apocalyptic literature often uses recapitulation — repeating the same spiritual realities through different visions & symbols rather than a strict chronological sequence.
individualism:
[Back]

Western culture highly values the individual, leading many readers to interpret the text's warnings, blessings & calls to endurance through a personal lens (eg. 'How does this affect my personal salvation or my future?'). However, John wrote to seven specific, corporate faith communities in Asia Minor. The text addresses systemic compromise, injustice & the collective witness of the Church against empire rather than just individual piety.
literalism:
[Back]

Influenced by the scientific revolution & Enlightenment thinking, Western minds tend to equate 'truth' with literal, historical, or scientific data. This leads to trying to decode symbols as literal objects (eg. interpreting locusts as attack helicopters or the beast as a specific modern politician). To the first-century reader, apocalyptic language was a standard genre where symbols communicated theological & political realities, not literal blueprints.
political:
[Back]

Western Christians frequently read Revelation through the lens of modern global geopolitics, assuming the text directly predicts the actions of the United States, Russia, China, or the modern Middle East. This overlooks the fact that the book was a direct critique of the Roman Empire of John's day & a universal warning against any human empire that elevates itself to the status of God.
escapism:
[Back]

Mainstream Western evangelicalism — particularly in North America — has been heavily influenced by 19th-century dispensationalism. This view assumes the primary goal of the book is to outline how Christians will be 'raptured' out of the world before suffering occurs. Conversely, the text itself focuses heavily on faithfulness through suffering & the ultimate renewal of this creation (with the New Jerusalem coming down to Earth) rather than an escape from it.
feelings: A lot of Christians - especially those who have grown up in certain conservative traditions - have mixed feelings about the Apocalypse. Fear is common … fear of the startling visions, or of the obsessions &/or dread they can provoke.
whole: Reading the whole book through should take less than 90 minutes even if you read it aloud, which the author seems to encourage us to do! (cf. 1:3)
introduction: The pages that provide an overview of the Jewish, Roman & Christian contexts that is very important. Having these contexts in mind makes it much more possible for us to 'hear' & feel the impact each scene in the Apocalypse would have made on those first-century readers. It may also help us avoid reading our own assumptions & meanings into the text!
outline: It is important to get a sense of the narrative arc, the major characters, the various scenes, the repeating themes & the overall structure … this will help keep your bearings when you focus on each specific passage.
start: Resist the temptation of skipping ahead to more 'exciting' sections! To understand this revelation, this 'apocalypse', rightly means reading it as the author clearly intended.
format:
Each passage in the guide is considered on a separate page.

The text is taken out of the 'verse & paragraph' formats of modern translations & arranged using a 'visual mapping' approach that aligns & groups related concepts & terms. This makes it easier for modern readers to read the text with 'fresh' eyes, & to identify connections & trends that would have been apparent & significant for the original audience.

This is particularly helpful in coming to grips with biblical texts (including the Apocalypse) where parallelism & linkages are frequently used to emphasise, develop & extend key ideas.
download:
You can print this off to make your own notes (or annotate the PDF directly on your device, if you prefer). You will see that room is provided to allow notes (from the comments &/or your own thoughts & insights) to be easily added.

On the guide pages for some passages there will also be an 'example annotation' link to an example of my annotations for that passage. Of course, this is just provided as a model for how to go about this process, not as something you should just copy without 'chewing your own food'!
highlighted:
Within the passage text (& at times in the passage headings) you will see some words &/or phrases highlighted with a light yellow box … like those on this page!

Select those highlights to see specific information (appearing in the right column alongside the text) relevant to how the first readers would have understood these terms. There may also be additional blue links within the comments on the right which you may follow to access more detailed information.

These comments are formatted to be quite compact & not overwhelming. The sub-links are then provided to allow readers to 'choose their own adventure', accessing as much detailed information as they wish.
questions:
This is really where we move from reading the verses & gaining information/insights to 'hearing what the Spirit is saying to the churches.'

Hearing the questions the Apocalypse is asking us — & with the Spirit's help, beginning to answer those questions in our own souls & lives — is when we begin growing in wisdom!
feedback:
At the bottom right of each page, there is a 'feedback &/or suggestions' link. Use this to give me any ideas regarding how that page could be improved.

This is a 'living' site which I expect to be constantly improving, so all feedback, suggestions & even criticisms are very welcome! My hope is that this guide may become increasingly useful to all comers & I'd be glad to receive your thoughts on how to make it excellent. 🙂
